summary.traveler: Travellers entering Jordan with JOD 10,000 or more, or the equivalent in foreign currency, must declare this to Jordanian customs. There is no restriction on the amount of foreign currency that may be brought into Jordan. Travellers may take out unlimited foreign currency but must declare amounts above JOD 10,000 or equivalent. The Jordanian dinar is pegged to the US dollar at 0.708 JOD per USD, a rate maintained since 1995 by the Central Bank of Jordan (CBJ).
summary.business: Jordan operates a relatively open foreign exchange regime administered by the Central Bank of Jordan (CBJ) under the Foreign Exchange Law. Current account transactions are broadly liberalised. Capital account transactions may require CBJ registration or approval for large flows. Businesses may hold foreign currency accounts at CBJ-authorised banks. The Jordanian dinar has maintained its peg to the USD since 1995, providing exchange rate stability. AML obligations apply under the Anti-Money Laundering and Counter Terrorism Financing Law.

rules.bring_foreign_currency_in: Travellers may bring any amount of foreign currency into Jordan. Amounts of JOD 10,000 or more (or the equivalent in foreign currency) must be declared to Jordanian Customs at entry. The declaration is made on the customs declaration form at ports of entry. Failure to declare amounts above the threshold may result in confiscation and penalties under Jordanian customs and AML legislation. No prior approval is required to bring in any amount of foreign currency.
rules.take_foreign_currency_out: Travellers may export foreign currency up to the amount declared and documented on arrival. Amounts of JOD 10,000 or more in foreign currency or bearer negotiable instruments must be declared to Customs upon departure under AML Law No. 20 of 2021. Jordanian dinars (JOD) may be exported up to JOD 300 per person only. Larger outward transfers of foreign currency must be conducted through CBJ-authorised banks. False declaration or failure to declare is subject to legal action under Jordanian anti-money laundering law. Source: customs.gov.jo; CBJ Foreign Currency Instructions.
rules.cash_declaration_threshold: The cash declaration threshold in Jordan is JOD 10,000 (or its equivalent in foreign currency). This is mandatory under Article 23-A of the Anti-Money Laundering and Counter-Terrorist Financing Law No. 20 of 2021. The declaration applies at both arrival and departure, covering cash and bearer negotiable instruments (BNI). At Queen Alia International Airport (QAIA), travellers carrying JOD 10,000 or more must proceed to the Customs Office next to the security checkpoint. Jordanian dinars (JOD) may be imported in unlimited amounts but only JOD 300 may be exported. Foreign currency may be imported in unlimited amounts when declared; the same amount may be exported, supported by the declaration record. Israeli sheqels are prohibited. Source: CBJ Foreign Currency Instructions; customs.gov.jo; AML Law No. 20/2021.
rules.resident_holding_rules: Jordanian residents may freely hold foreign currency accounts at CBJ-authorised banks. Residents may purchase foreign currency for authorised purposes through the banking system. The CBJ maintains the JOD peg to the USD, which provides stability for residents holding dinars. No general restrictions apply to holding foreign currency, but large capital outflows require CBJ-registered banking channels.
rules.non_resident_rules: Non-residents may hold foreign currency accounts at Jordanian banks and freely transfer funds in and out of Jordan through the banking system. Foreign investors may repatriate profits, dividends, and capital without restriction, subject to documentation. Jordan has signed investment protection agreements with numerous countries that reinforce repatriation rights. Non-residents must comply with AML and KYC requirements at Jordanian banks.
rules.business_invoicing_settlement: Jordanian businesses may invoice and settle international transactions in foreign currencies through CBJ-authorised banks. No mandatory conversion requirements exist for foreign exchange receipts from exports. Large capital account transactions — including foreign investment flows and loan disbursements — should be processed through the banking system with CBJ registration where required. AML obligations apply under the Anti-Money Laundering and Counter Terrorism Financing Law administered by the Anti-Money Laundering and Counter Terrorism Financing Unit (AML/CTF Unit).
rules.exchange_controls: Jordan maintains a largely open foreign exchange regime with the Jordanian dinar pegged to the US dollar at 0.708 JOD per USD since 1995. The CBJ manages the peg through foreign exchange reserves. No general capital controls apply. Current account transactions are liberalised. Large capital flows by residents and businesses should be conducted through CBJ-authorised channels. AML monitoring applies under the CBJ's financial supervision framework. Sanctions compliance obligations apply for dealings with internationally designated parties.
rules.banking_conversion_practicality: Foreign currency exchange is available through CBJ-authorised commercial banks and licensed exchange companies in Jordan. ATMs accepting international cards are available in Amman and major cities. The JOD/USD peg provides a stable, predictable exchange rate for travellers and businesses. Exchange companies are regulated by the CBJ. International transfers are processed via SWIFT through authorised Jordanian banks. Currency exchange in rural areas may be limited.
